title: Building a Universe of Local Rules
concept_layer: cellular automata; local rules → global emergence; discrete time + discrete space; state update from neighbors
domain_deferred: edge of chaos / Langton's λ → CA_EdgeOfChaos

capture_leaks.deterministic_rule: Conway's B3/S23 is fixed. Totalistic, outer-totalistic, probabilistic rules are all variations. The rule is one choice in a vast space.
capture_leaks.synchronous_update: All cells update simultaneously, based on the previous state. Asynchronous (each cell updates at its own time) gives different emergent behavior.
capture_leaks.moore_neighborhood: Eight neighbors (square + diagonals). Von Neumann (4), hexagonal (6), extended (radius r), 3D (26). Topology shapes outcomes.
capture_leaks.boundary_conditions: What about the edges? Wrap-around (torus), dead (walls), reflect (mirror). Each changes long-run behavior. This map wraps.
capture_leaks.no_influence_from_afar: A glider at (0,0) cannot affect (100,100) faster than 100 generations. CA are strictly local. Long-range phenomena (gravity, light) need different machinery.
capture_leaks.irreversibility: Given the current state, we can compute the next — but many past states lead here. Time is one-way. Reversibility requires more bits per cell.

limit: A 20×20 grid, one rule, pure local logic. The artifact shows that complex global behavior emerges from trivially-local rules. What it refuses: causality from outside the grid, non-square topology, variable rules, continuous values. It is one step along the computational-universality ladder: elementary CA (1D) → Life (2D) → Turing machine (1D tape with read/write head) → lambda calculus. The grid is a computer the player can watch thinking.

grammar_alignment.note: 7_2_game_of_life_vr teaches step (advance one generation) and evolve (run many generations). The rule is hardcoded here — rule parameterization is the job of CA_ElementaryRules. Seed patterns (glider, pulsar, R-pentomino) are taught by a dedicated pattern loader artifact.

biome_alignment.note: Big shift — density crosses 0.5 (world is becoming alive). 'cellular' catalyst lets the player apply local rules to any surface. Flowers and fungus arrange via CA-like rules now; vegetation patches form organically. The world is literally running cellular automata as its growth algorithm.

stages.title: From noise to rule
stages.thinking: Perlin noise produces terrain from neighbor correlation — a rule that says 'agree gently.' Now a stricter rule, and a surprise: sharp discrete rules can produce behavior more complex than noise, not less. A cell is alive or dead. It has 8 neighbors. Three rules decide its fate. That's the entire system. Gliders, oscillators, replicators, universal computation — all from those three rules. Emergence from local logic is the subject of this sequence.
stages.code:
# Noise: gradient sum, smooth blending, continuous values
# CA: binary cell, discrete time, three rules
#
# Conway's B3/S23 (Game of Life):
#   Birth:     dead cell with exactly 3 neighbors → alive
#   Survive:   alive cell with 2 or 3 neighbors → stays alive
#   Die:       all other cases → dead
#
# Three rules. Infinite complexity.
# This is the deepest claim of the CA sequence.

stages.title: Store the grid as a packed array
stages.thinking: A 20×20 grid has 400 cells. Each cell needs one bit (alive/dead). PackedByteArray is Godot's efficient byte storage. One byte per cell is overkill for a bit but simplifies indexing. The grid is stored, updated, read, rendered every tick. Storing two grids (current and next) enables double-buffering: compute the next state from the current without overwriting.

stages.title: Count alive neighbors — the atomic query
stages.thinking: For each cell, look at 8 surrounding cells and count how many are alive. Wrap around at edges (torus topology — what leaves the right comes in the left). This count determines the cell's fate. The neighbor-count function is the heart of every CA — different rules just map count-and-current-state to next-state differently.
stages.code:
func _count_neighbors(x: int, y: int) -> int:
	var count = 0
	for dy in [-1, 0, 1]:
		for dx in [-1, 0, 1]:
			if dx == 0 and dy == 0:
				continue  # skip self
			# Wrap around edges (torus)
			var nx = (x + dx + grid_size) % grid_size
			var ny = (y + dy + grid_size) % grid_size
			count += _cells[ny][nx]
	return count

# 3 lines do the topology work.
# Modulo + offset = wrap-around.
# This would break if the grid were infinite.
# Wrap is the CHEAP fix; truth is more complex.

stages.title: Apply the B3/S23 rule
stages.thinking: This is Conway's entire universe in four lines. A dead cell with exactly 3 neighbors becomes alive (birth). A living cell with 2 or 3 neighbors stays alive (survival). Every other case: dead. Change `[3]` to `[3, 6]` and you get HighLife, which has replicators that Life doesn't. Change the numbers and you change the physics of the universe.

stages.title: Run the rule every update_interval seconds
stages.thinking: The grid doesn't update every frame — it updates every update_interval. This is a deliberate choice. Too fast: the eye can't track emergence. Too slow: the player gets bored. 0.4 seconds per generation lets the player see individual events (a glider taking one step) while also watching long-term patterns form. Time discretization is a critical pedagogical choice.

stages.title: Render cells as a grid of materials
stages.thinking: Two materials: alive (pink) and dead (translucent glass). For each cell, set material based on state. At 400 cells and 0.4 seconds per update, performance is trivial. For larger grids, MultiMeshInstance3D is the pattern — one mesh, hundreds of transforms, single draw call. The artifact uses a simpler per-cell approach because readability trumps performance at teaching scale.

stages.title: Let the player inject initial conditions
stages.thinking: A slider for alive_probability. Low values (5%): mostly dead, few survivors, tiny glimmers. Medium (30%): rich interactions, gliders emerge. High (80%): dense clumps that mostly die from overcrowding. The player tunes the initial density and watches different universes play out. Each universe has the SAME RULE. Different initial conditions are different STORIES of the same physics.
stages.code:
var probability_controller := CONTROLLER_SCENE.instantiate()
probability_controller.parameter_name = "Alive %"
probability_controller.min_value = 0.05
probability_controller.max_value = 0.9
probability_controller.default_value = alive_probability
probability_controller.value_changed.connect(func(v: float) -> void:
	alive_probability = v
	# Rebuild initial grid with new probability
	_initialize_grid()
	_generation = 1
)

# Same rule, different seeds, different stories.
# Chaos theory in a grid.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: The Game of Life knows what it is. Not a toy grid — a proof that complexity arises from simplicity. The rule is trivial; the behaviors are inexhaustible. Gliders glide. Oscillators pulse. R-pentominoes evolve for 1,103 generations before settling. Gospers discovered a glider gun that emits gliders forever. All from the same four lines of code. The Life grid is a window into why the universe can be at once law-abiding and surprising. What it refuses: continuity, long-range forces, variable rules, rich cell states. Those are doors to the rest of the sequence.
stages.code:
# @identity
# essence: 20×20 grid of binary cells updated by Conway's B3/S23 rule — dead cells with 3 neighbors come alive, alive cells with 2 or 3 neighbors survive, all else die
# desire: learner watches patterns emerge, die, oscillate, glide — and realizes the rule is three lines and the behavior is inexhaustible
# critical_parameter: alive_probability — initial density controls which universe of behaviors unfolds
# triggers: timer ticks every update_interval, _step() computes next state, _render_cells() updates visual, _update_status() reports generation count
# emerges: gliders, oscillators, still-lifes, chaos regions — all from three local rules with no global coordination
# needs: PackedByteArray grid [has]; material swap rendering [has]; probability slider [has]; reset [missing explicit]
# relationships: 2D case of elementary CA (CA_ElementaryRules = 1D version); feeds CA_BeyondBinary (more states), CA_ExpandingSpace (larger scale), fractals (Rule 90 → Sierpinski)
# truth: complexity is cheap — a universe obeying three rules can host an infinity of stories
